summary: For constant α: ω = ω0 + α t, θ = ω0 t + (1)/(2)α t^2, ω^2 = ω0^2 + 2αθ; and s = rθ, v = rω, at = rα, ac = rω^2.
Rotational kinetic energy Ek = (1)/(2)Iω^2, where I = Σ mi ri^2 = ∫ r^2dm is the moment of inertia.
Radius of gyration: I = Mk^2, so k = √I/M. Parallel axis: I = Icm + Md^2; perpendicular axis (laminae): Iz = Ix + Iy.
Uniform rod of mass M, length L: I = ML^2/12 about the centre and ML^2/3 about one end.
Torque τ = rFsinφ and τ = Iα, the rotational form of F = ma.
Work W = τθ, power P = τω, and W = (1)/(2)Iω2^2 - (1)/(2)Iω1^2.
Angular momentum L = Iω with τ = dL/dt. If τ = 0 then I1ω1 = I2ω2: angular momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy need not be.

sections.title: Application of SHM: vertical oscillation of mass suspended from coiled spring
Oscillatory motion: Damped oscillation, Forced oscillation and resonance

summary: SHM: a = -ω^2x, with x = Asin(ω t + φ), v = Aωcos(ω t+φ) = ω√A^2-x^2 and T = 2π/ω = 2π√m/k.
Speed is maximum (Aω) at the mean position; acceleration is maximum (ω^2A) at the extremes. SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter.
U = (1)/(2)mω^2x^2, K = (1)/(2)mω^2(A^2-x^2), and the total E = (1)/(2)mω^2A^2 = (1)/(2)kA^2 is constant.
Mass on a vertical spring: mg = ke and T = 2π√m/k = 2π√e/g; the weight only shifts the mean position.
Angular SHM: τ = -cθ gives T = 2π√I/c. Simple pendulum: T = 2π√L/g for small amplitude, independent of the mass of the bob.
Damped oscillation: A = A0e^-bt/2m, ω' = √k/m - b^2/4m^2; critical damping returns the system to rest fastest.
A forced oscillator vibrates at the driver's frequency; at resonance (ωd = ω0) the amplitude is maximum and is limited only by damping.

summary: P = hρ g (gauge), P = P0 + hρ g (absolute); pressure depends on depth only, and Pascal's law transmits it undiminished.
Upthrust U = Vρ g = weight of fluid displaced; a floating body has Vs/V = ρb/ρl.
T = F/L (N m⁻¹) equals the surface energy W/Δ A (J m⁻²). Excess pressure: 2T/r in a drop, 4T/r in a soap bubble.
Capillary rise h = 2Tcosθ/rρ g, so h ∝ 1/r.
Viscosity F = η A dv/dx, η in Pa s, [ML^-1T^-1].
Poiseuille Q = π P r^4/8η l — the fourth power of the radius.
Stokes F = 6πη rv, giving vt = 2r^2(ρ-σ)g/9η.
Continuity A1v1 = A2v2 (mass) and Bernoulli P + (1)/(2)ρ v^2 + ρ gh = constant (energy), giving v = √2gh for efflux.

topics: Heat and work; Internal energy and First law of thermodynamics

sections.title: Heat and work; Internal energy and First law of thermodynamics
Thermodynamic processes: Adiabatic, isochoric, isothermal and isobaric
Heat capacities of an ideal gas at constant pressure and volume and relation between them
Isothermal and Adiabatic processes for an ideal gas

summary: A system exchanges matter and energy with its surroundings across a boundary; open, closed and isolated systems differ in what may cross it. P, V, T and U are state functions; Q and W are path functions.
Work done by a gas is W = ∫ P dV, the area under the P–V curve; positive for expansion, negative for compression.
First law: Q = Δ U + W, with Q positive for heat absorbed and W positive for expansion. For an ideal gas U depends only on T.
Isochoric: W=0, Q=Δ U. Isobaric: W = PΔ V. Isothermal: Δ U = 0, Q = W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, Δ U = -W. Cyclic: Δ U = 0, Q = W = area of loop.
Mayer's relation: Cp - Cv = R, so Cv = R/(γ-1) and Cp = γ R/(γ-1). Here γ = 1.67, 1.40 and 1.33 for mono-, di- and polyatomic gases.
Isothermal: PV = constant and W = nRTln(V2/V1).
Adiabatic: PV^γ = constant, TV^γ-1 = constant, and W = (P1V1 - P2V2)/(γ-1) = nR(T1-T2)/(γ-1).
At any common point the adiabatic curve is γ times steeper than the isothermal, so adiabatic expansion cools a gas.

units.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
topics: Thermodynamic systems and direction of thermodynamic processes
Internal combustion engines: Otto cycle, Diesel cycle, Carnot cycle

sections.title: Thermodynamic systems and direction of thermodynamic processes
Internal combustion engines: Otto cycle, Diesel cycle, Carnot cycle

summary: Real processes run one way only. A reversible process is quasi-static and free of all dissipative effects; no real process is reversible.

Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic device can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work. Clausius: no self-acting cyclic device can move heat from a colder to a hotter body. The two statements are equivalent.
Heat engine: W = Q1 - Q2 and η = W/Q1 = 1 - Q2/Q1. A sink is compulsory, so η < 1 always.
Otto cycle (petrol): two adiabatics and two isochorics, η = 1 - r^-(γ-1). Diesel cycle: heat added isobarically, allowing a much larger r.
Carnot cycle: two isothermals and two adiabatics, all reversible, with η = 1 - T2/T1 — the maximum possible for the given temperatures, and independent of the working substance (Carnot's theorem).
Refrigerator: Q1 = Q2 + W, β = Q2/W = Q2/(Q1-Q2), and for the ideal case βmax = T2/(T1-T2) = (1-η)/η.
Entropy dS = dQrev/T is a state function measured in J K⁻¹, and for an isothermal change Δ S = Q/T. The second law states Δ Suniverse ≥ 0; entropy is a measure of disorder.

units.title: Wave motion
summary: A progressive wave carries energy and momentum through a medium without carrying the medium. Transverse waves vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel, longitudinal waves parallel to it.
v = fλ = λ/T for every wave; in a given medium v is fixed, so raising f shortens λ.
Wave equation: y = asin(ω t - kx) = asin 2π(t/T - x/λ), with ω = 2π/T, k = 2π/λ and v = ω/k. Use +kx for a wave travelling in the -x direction.
Phase difference and path difference are linked by Δφ = (2π/λ)Δ x.
Particle velocity vp = aωcos(ω t - kx), maximum aω; it is not the wave velocity.
Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose to give a stationary wave, y = 2acos kx sinω t, whose amplitude 2acos(2π x/λ) depends on position.
Nodes (zero amplitude) lie at x = λ/4, 3λ/4, ldots and antinodes (amplitude 2a) at x = 0, λ/2, λ, ldots. Successive nodes are λ/2 apart and a node is λ/4 from the nearest antinode.

units.title: Mechanical waves
topics: Speed of wave motion; Velocity of sound in solid and liquid
Effect of temperature, pressure, humidity on velocity of sound

sections.title: Speed of wave motion; velocity of sound in solid and liquid
Effect of temperature, pressure, humidity on velocity of sound

summary: Every wave obeys v=fλ, but the speed itself is set by the medium: v=√E/ρ, elasticity over inertia.
Solid rod: v=√Y/ρ (≈ 5060 m s^-1 in steel). Liquid: v=√B/ρ (≈ 1480 m s^-1 in water). Fluids carry only longitudinal sound; solids carry longitudinal and transverse waves.
Newton's formula: assuming isothermal compressions, Biso=P and v=√P/ρ, giving 280 m s⁻¹ for air — 16 % too low.
Laplace's correction: the compressions are adiabatic, so Badi=γ P and v=√γ P/ρ = 331 m s^-1, which matches experiment.
Eliminating density gives v=√γ RT/M: the speed depends on temperature and on the gas, never on the pressure.
vt=v0√1+t/273≈ v0+0.61t for air: +0.61 m s⁻¹ per °C.
Humidity raises v slightly (moist air is lighter); wind adds vectorially, veff=v+wcosθ; amplitude and frequency have no effect.
terms: Newton's general formula for wave speed

units.title: Wave in pipes and strings
topics: Stationary waves in closed and open pipes
Harmonics and overtones in closed and open organ pipes
Velocity of transverse waves along a stretched string
Laws of vibration of fixed string

sections.title: Stationary waves in closed and open pipes
Harmonics and overtones in closed and open organ pipes
Velocity of transverse waves along a stretched string
Laws of vibration of fixed string

summary: A stationary wave forms when incident and reflected waves superpose. Closed end → displacement node; open end → displacement antinode. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart.
Closed pipe: L=(2n-1)λ/4, so fn = (2n-1)v/4L — odd harmonics only. The 1st overtone is the 3rd harmonic.
Open pipe: L=nλ/2, so fn = nv/2L — all harmonics. An open pipe sounds one octave above a closed pipe of the same length and gives a richer note.
End correction e = 0.6r: closed pipe f1 = v/4(L+e), open pipe f1 = v/2(L+2e).
Resonance tube: v = 2f(l2-l1) and e = (l2-3l1)/2.
Transverse waves on a string: v = √T/μ, derived from the centripetal force on a curved element.
String fixed at both ends: fn = dfracn2L√dfracTμ, all harmonics present.
Laws of a vibrating string: f∝ 1/L, f∝√T, f∝ 1/√μ.

units.title: Acoustic phenomena
topics: Characteristics of sound: Intensity, loudness, quality and pitch

sections.title: Characteristics of sound: intensity, loudness, quality and pitch

summary: Excess pressure Δ P = -B partial y/partial x; the pressure amplitude is P0 = Bak = ρ vω a = 2πρ v f a.
The pressure wave is λ/4 out of phase with the displacement wave: a displacement node is a pressure antinode.
Intensity I = (1)/(2)ρ vω^2a^2 = P0^2/2ρ v, in W m⁻²; for a point source I = P/4π r^2, so I∝ 1/r^2.
Intensity level β = 10log10(I/I0) dB with I0 = 10^-12 W m^-2. Doubling I adds 3 dB; doubling the distance subtracts 6 dB.
Loudness (Weber–Fechner, L = klog I) is the sensation; pitch is set by frequency; quality is set by the overtones present, i.e. by the waveform.
Doppler effect: f' = dfracv+vov-vsf, with vo and vs counted positive when the motion brings source and observer closer.
There is no Doppler shift for motion perpendicular to the line of sight, for equal velocities in the same direction, or for a steady wind.

units.title: Nature and propagation of light
topics: Reflection and Refraction according to wave theory

sections.title: Reflection and Refraction according to wave theory

summary: A wavefront is the locus of points vibrating in the same phase; a ray is the normal to the wavefront. Wavefronts may be spherical, cylindrical or plane.

Huygens' principle: every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets of radius vt; the new wavefront is their forward envelope. Backward wavelets are suppressed by the obliquity factor K = (1)/(2)(1+cosθ).
Reflection: BC = AD = ct gives sin i/sin r = 1, so i = r, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal are coplanar.
Refraction: BC = v1t, AD = v2t give dfracsin isin r = dfracv1v2 = dfracn2n1, i.e. n1sin i = n2sin r.
On refraction the frequency is unchanged; the speed and wavelength both fall by the factor n: v = c/n and λm = λ0/n.
Optical path = n × geometrical path; it is the vacuum distance holding the same number of waves.
The wave theory predicts vwater < vair, confirmed by Foucault in 1850; the corpuscular theory predicted the opposite and failed.

units.title: Interference
summary: Superposition gives I = I1 + I2 + 2√I1I2cosφ, with φ = 2πΔ/λ.
Bright when Δ = nλ; dark when Δ = (2n-1)λ/2. For equal sources I = 4I0cos^2(φ/2), with Imax = 4I0, Imin = 0.
Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference; they must be obtained from one source, by division of wavefront or of amplitude.
In Young's experiment Δ = yd/D, bright fringes at yn = nλ D/d, dark at yn = (2n-1)λ D/2d.
Fringe width β = λ D/d; all fringes are equally spaced and equally bright. In a medium of index n, β shrinks to β/n.
Energy is redistributed, not destroyed: the average intensity across the pattern is 2I0, exactly what the two beams carry.

units.title: Diffraction
topics: Diffraction pattern of image; Diffraction grating

sections.title: Diffraction pattern of image; Diffraction grating

summary: Diffraction is the bending of light round edges, noticeable only when the aperture is comparable with λ. Fraunhofer diffraction uses plane waves.
Single slit minima: asinθ = nλ for n = ±1, ±2, dots; secondary maxima near asinθ = (n+(1)/(2))λ, of relative intensity 4.7%, 1.7%, …
Intensity: I = I0(sinβ/β)^2 with β = π asinθ/λ.
Central maximum: angular width 2λ/a, linear width 2λ D/a — it gets wider as the slit gets narrower.
Grating element d = 1/N; grating equation dsinθ = nλ; highest order nmax = d/λ; in each order violet is deviated least.
Rayleigh criterion: just resolved when one central maximum sits on the other's first minimum.
Telescope: θmin = 1.22λ/a, R.P. = a/1.22λ. Microscope: xmin = 1.22λ/2μsinθ. Grating: λ/dλ = nN.

units.title: Polarization
topics: Brewster's law; transverse nature of light

sections.title: Brewster's law; transverse nature of light

summary: Unpolarized light vibrates in all directions perpendicular to the ray; plane polarized light vibrates in one plane only. The plane of polarization is perpendicular to the plane of vibration.
Polarized light is produced by reflection, refraction through a pile of plates, selective absorption (Polaroid), double refraction (Nicol prism) and scattering.
Degree of polarization P = (Imax-Imin)/(Imax+Imin).
Brewster's law: n = tanθp, with θp + r = 90^°; the reflected and refracted rays are then perpendicular and the reflected beam is fully plane polarized.
Brewster's angle (tan^-1n, rarer to denser) is not the critical angle (sin^-1(1/n), denser to rarer).
Malus's law: I = I0cos^2θ. Unpolarized light through the first Polaroid always gives I0/2; crossed Polaroids give zero.
Polarization occurs for transverse waves only, so it proves that light is a transverse wave. Sound, being longitudinal, cannot be polarized.

units.title: Electrical circuits
topics: Potentiometer: Comparison of e.m.f.; measurement of internal resistance of a cell
Conversion of galvanometer into voltmeter and ammeter; Ohmmeter

sections.title: Potentiometer: Comparison of e.m.f.; measurement of internal resistance of a cell
Conversion of galvanometer into voltmeter and ammeter; Ohmmeter

summary: Kirchhoff's junction law Σ I = 0 expresses conservation of charge; the loop law Σ E = Σ IR expresses conservation of energy.
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when Ig = 0, and then P/Q = R/S. The condition is independent of the cell and of the galvanometer.
Metre bridge: X = R l/(100-l), with l measured from the end next to X. Keep l near 50 cm and interchange X and R to cancel end errors.
Potentiometer: V = kl with k = VAB/L. Comparison of e.m.f. E1/E2 = l1/l2; internal resistance r = R(l1-l2)/l2. At balance the cell supplies no current, so the true e.m.f. is measured.
A superconductor has ρ = 0 below Tc and expels magnetic flux (Meissner effect); a merely perfect conductor would trap the flux instead.
Galvanometer conversions: ammeter S = IgG/(I-Ig) in parallel; voltmeter R = V/Ig - G in series. An ohmmeter has a reversed, non-uniform scale.
Joule's law: H = I^2Rt = VIt = V^2t/R; power P = I^2R = V^2/R; 1 kWh = 3.6×10^6 J.

units.title: Thermoelectric effects
topics: Peltier effect: Variation of thermoelectric e.m.f. with temperature; Thermopile

sections.title: Peltier effect: Variation of thermoelectric e.m.f. with temperature; Thermopile

summary: Seebeck effect: two dissimilar metals, two junctions at different temperatures, an e.m.f. appears. It depends only on the metals and on the temperature difference.

Seebeck series Sb, Fe, Cd, Zn, Ag, Au, Cr, Sn, Pb, Hg, Mn, Cu, Pt, Co, Ni, Bi: the current flows from the earlier metal to the later one through the cold junction, and the further apart the metals, the greater the e.m.f.
Peltier effect: a current through a junction evolves heat at one junction and absorbs it at the other; H = π It, proportional to I and reversible, unlike Joule heat I^2Rt.
E = αθ + (1)/(2)βθ^2 with the cold junction at 0 ^°C; thermoelectric power S = dE/dθ = α + βθ.
Neutral temperature θn = -α/β (where E is maximum, fixed by the metals alone); temperature of inversion θi = 2θn - θc (where E returns to zero and reverses).
Emax = -α^2/2β, reached at θn.
A thermopile is many Sb–Bi couples in series, alternate junctions blackened, used to detect and measure heat radiation.

topics: Magnetic field lines and magnetic flux; Oersted's experiment
Force on moving charge; Force on a conductor
Force and Torque on rectangular coil; Moving coil galvanometer
Magnetic field of a moving charge
Biot and Savart law and application to circular coil, long straight conductor, long solenoid
Ampere's law and applications to long straight conductor, straight solenoid, toroidal solenoid
Force between two parallel conductors carrying current; definition of ampere

sections.title: Magnetic field lines and magnetic flux; Oersted's experiment
Force on moving charge; Force on a conductor
Force and Torque on rectangular coil; Moving coil galvanometer
Magnetic field of a moving charge
Biot and Savart law and application to circular coil, long straight conductor, long solenoid
Ampere's law and applications to long straight conductor, straight solenoid, toroidal solenoid
Force between two parallel conductors carrying current; definition of ampere

summary: Magnetic flux Phi = BAcosθ (weber); field lines are closed loops, so ointB· dA = 0 — there are no magnetic monopoles.
Oersted: a current produces a magnetic field. Direction by the right-hand grip rule (or SNOW).
Force on a moving charge F = qvtimesB, F = qvBsinθ; it does no work. Perpendicular entry gives a circle with r = mv/qB, T = 2π m/qB, independent of speed.
Force on a conductor F = BILsinθ; direction by Fleming's left-hand rule.
Torque on a coil τ = NBIAsinθ = NBIAcosα, with dipole moment m = NIA. A radial field makes sinθ = 1, so a moving-coil galvanometer has varphi = (NBA/c)I and a uniform scale.
Hall effect: VH = IB/nqt with RH = 1/nq; it gives the sign and the concentration of the carriers.
Biot–Savart: dB = (μ0/4π)(I dlsinθ/r^2). Results: straight wire μ0I/2π a; centre of a coil μ0NI/2a; on the axis μ0NIa^2/2(a^2+x^2)^3/2; long solenoid μ0nI (half that at an end).
Ampère: ointB· dl = μ0Ienc, which gives the straight wire, the solenoid (μ0nI) and the toroid (μ0NI/2π r, zero outside) in a few lines each.

units.title: Magnetic properties of materials
topics: Magnetic field lines and magnetic flux
Flux density in magnetic material; Relative permeability; Susceptibility

sections.title: Magnetic field lines and magnetic flux
Flux density in magnetic material; Relative permeability; Susceptibility

summary: Magnetic flux Phi = BAcosθ (weber); B = Phi/A is the flux density (tesla); ointB· dA = 0 since field lines are closed loops.
The magnetising field is H = NI/l (A m⁻¹); magnetisation is M = m/V (A m⁻¹); inside matter B = μ0(H+M).
chim = M/H, μ = B/H, μr = μ/μ0 and μr = 1 + chim. Both chim and μr are dimensionless.
Hysteresis is the lag of B behind H. Retentivity Br is the flux density left when H = 0; coercivity Hc is the reverse field that makes B = 0.
Energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle equals the loop area, oint H dB (J m⁻³); the hysteresis power loss is (area) × V × f.
Soft materials (small Hc, narrow loop) are for transformer cores and electromagnets; hard materials (large Hc, broad loop) are for permanent magnets.

Diamagnetics: chim small negative, μr < 1, repelled. Paramagnetics: chim small positive, μr > 1, chim = C/T. Ferromagnetics: domains, chim gg 1, saturation and hysteresis, and chim = C/(T - TC) above the Curie temperature.

units.title: Electromagnetic Induction
summary: Faraday: an e.m.f. appears whenever flux linkage changes, e = -N dPhi/dt; the charge circulated is q = NΔPhi/R, independent of the time taken.
A changing B produces a non-conservative induced electric field, ointE· dl = -dPhi/dt.
Lenz: the induced current opposes the change producing it — a statement of energy conservation, carried by the minus sign.
Motional e.m.f. e = Blv (or Blvsinθ); the retarding force is B^2l^2v/R and Fv = I^2R.
A.C. generator: Phi = BAcosω t gives e = NBAωsinω t with peak value e0 = NBAω.
Eddy currents are reduced by laminating cores; they are used in induction furnaces, induction cookers and electromagnetic brakes.
L = NPhi/I, e = -L dI/dt, solenoid L = μ0μrN^2A/l; M = k√L1L2 and e2 = -M dI1/dt. Unit: henry.
Energy stored U = (1)/(2)LI^2; energy density u = B^2/2μ0.

units.title: Alternating Currents
topics: Peak and rms value of AC current and voltage
AC through a resistor, a capacitor and an inductor
Series circuits containing combination of resistance, capacitance and inductance
Power in AC circuits: power factor

sections.title: Peak and rms value of AC current and voltage
AC through a resistor, a capacitor and an inductor
Series circuits containing combination of resistance, capacitance and inductance
Power in AC circuits: power factor

summary: For i = I0sinω t: Irms = I0/√2 = 0.707I0, Iav (half cycle) = 2I0/π = 0.637I0, and the full-cycle mean is zero. Meters read r.m.s.
Resistor: i in phase with v. Inductor: i lags by 90^°, XL = 2π fL. Capacitor: i leads by 90^°, XC = 1/2π fC.
A phasor is a vector of length equal to the peak (or r.m.s.) value, rotating at ω; sinusoids of the same frequency add like vectors.
Series LCR: Z = √R^2+(XL-XC)^2 and tanφ = (XL-XC)/R; V = √VR^2+(VL-VC)^2.
Resonance: XL = XC, so f0 = 1/2π√LC, Zmin = R, Imax = V/R and φ = 0 (acceptor circuit).
Quality factor Q = ω0L/R = (1/R)√L/C = f0/Δ f = VL/V; a large Q means a sharp resonance and a narrow bandwidth.
Power: Pav = VrmsIrmscosφ, with power factor cosφ = R/Z. Pure L or C consumes no power — wattless current.

units.title: Electrons
topics: Motion of electron beam in electric and magnetic fields
Thomson's experiment to determine specific charge of electrons

sections.title: Motion of electron beam in electric and magnetic fields
Thomson's experiment to determine specific charge of electrons

summary: Millikan balanced the apparent weight of a charged oil drop against an electric force: q = mgd/V for a stationary drop, or q = 6πη r v1 d/V with r = √9η v1/2(ρ-σ)g.
Every measured charge is an integral multiple of e = 1.60×10^-19 C: charge is quantised.
An electron accelerated through Va has speed v = √2eVa/m.
In a transverse electric field the path is a parabola with deflection y = eEL^2/2mv^2 = VdL^2/4Vad at the edge of the plates.
In a transverse magnetic field the path is a circle, r = mv/eB, period T = 2π m/eB; the magnetic force does no work, so the speed is unchanged.
Crossed fields select one speed: v = E/B.
Thomson's tube gives e/m = E/B^2r = 2yE/B^2L^2; the accepted value is 1.76×10^11 C kg^-1, which with Millikan's e gives m = 9.11×10^-31 kg.

units.title: Photons
summary: Radiation is emitted and absorbed in quanta: a photon has E = hf = hc/λ, p = h/λ, zero rest mass, and travels at c.
Intensity fixes the number of photons per second; frequency fixes the energy of each one.
Photoelectric emission occurs only above a threshold frequency f0, is instantaneous, gives a current proportional to intensity, and gives a maximum kinetic energy proportional to (f-f0).
Einstein's equation: hf = φ0 + Kmax, with φ0 = hf0 = hc/λ0.
Stopping potential: eV0 = Kmax, so V0 = (h/e)f - φ0/e; V0 is independent of intensity.
A graph of V0 against f is a straight line of slope h/e, intercept -φ0/e and f-intercept f0; the slope is the same for every metal, giving h = 6.63×10^-34 J s.

units.title: Semiconductor devices
topics: Semiconductor diode: Characteristics in forward and reverse bias
Logic gates: NOT, OR, AND, NAND and NOR

sections.title: Semiconductor diode: Characteristics in forward and reverse bias
Logic gates: NOT, OR, AND, NAND and NOR
The junction transistor and its configurations

summary: Diffusion across a p-n junction leaves a depletion region of immobile ions and a barrier potential VB (0.3 V Ge, 0.7 V Si) that stops further diffusion.

Forward bias lowers the barrier, narrows the depletion layer and gives a large majority-carrier current; reverse bias does the opposite and leaves only a microamp reverse saturation current until breakdown.
The diode characteristic is non-linear: no current below the knee voltage, then a steep rise. Dynamic resistance rd = Δ V/Δ I.
Half-wave: Idc=Im/π, ηmax=40.6%, ripple 1.21, output 50 Hz.
Full-wave: Idc=2Im/π, Vdc=2Vm/π, Irms=Im/√2, η = (8/π^2)RL/(RL+rf), maximum 81.2%, ripple 0.48, output 100 Hz.
PIV is Vm for half-wave and bridge, 2Vm for the centre-tap circuit.
Gates: OR gives 0 only for all-zero inputs; AND gives 1 only for all-one inputs; NAND and NOR are their complements and are universal gates.
Transistor: IE = IB + IC, α = IC/IE, β = IC/IB = α/(1-α).

units.title: Quantization of energy

summary: Bohr: mvr = nh/2π; rn = varepsilon0h^2n^2/π me^2 = 0.529 n^2 Å; vn = c/137n; En = -13.6/n^2 eV (multiply by Z^2, divide rn by Z, for hydrogen-like ions).
hν = Ei - Ef gives 1/λ = R(1/nf^2 - 1/ni^2), R = 1.097×10^7 m⁻¹. Series: Lyman (UV, nf=1), Balmer (visible), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (IR).
Hydrogen: first excitation potential 10.2 V, ionization potential 13.6 V. Emission gives bright lines, absorption dark lines at the same wavelengths.
De Broglie: λ = h/p = 12.27/√V Å for an accelerated electron; 2π r = nλ reproduces Bohr's quantization.
Uncertainty: Δ x Δ p ≥ h/4π and Δ E Δ t ≥ h/4π.
X-ray tube: continuous spectrum with λmin = hc/eV (depends on V) plus characteristic Kα, Kβ lines (depend on the target).
Bragg: 2dsinθ = nλ, θ measured from the atomic plane.

topics: Medical use of nuclear radiation and possible health hazard

sections.title: Medical use of nuclear radiation and possible health hazard

summary: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near A ≈ 56 at about 8.8 MeV; nuclei move towards the peak by fusing, splitting or emitting α-particles.
α = ⁴₂He (A-4, Z-2); β^- = electron created when n → p (Z+1); γ = photon (no change). Ionizing power α > β > γ; penetrating power is the reverse.
Q = Δ m × 931.5 MeV is the energy released in a decay.
Decay law: dN/dt = -λ N gives N = N0e^-λ t and A = λ N = A0e^-λ t. 1 Ci = 3.7×10^10 Bq.
T1/2 = 0.693/λ; τ = 1/λ = 1.44 T1/2; after n half-lives N/N0 = (1/2)^n.
A GM tube uses avalanche ionization in argon at 400 V, with a quenching vapour and a dead time of about 200 μs; it counts particles but not their energy.
Carbon dating: t = (T1/2/0.693)ln(A0/A) with A0 = 15.3 min⁻¹ g⁻¹ and T1/2 = 5730 y; useful to about 50,000 years.
Medical tracers are short-lived γ-emitters; therapy uses cobalt-60. Dose is measured in gray (absorbed) and sievert (equivalent).

sections.title: Seismology: Surface waves (Rayleigh and Love waves); Internal waves (S and P-waves); Wave patterns of Gorkha Earthquake 2015

summary: Body waves: P (longitudinal, ~6 km s⁻¹, passes through liquids) and S (transverse, ~3.5 km s⁻¹, blocked by liquids). Surface waves: Love (horizontal transverse) and Rayleigh (rolling ellipse, largest amplitude). Arrival order P, S, Love, Rayleigh.
Epicentral distance from the S–P interval: d = Δ t vPvS/(vP - vS); three stations fix the epicentre.

Gorkha: 25 April 2015, Mw 7.8, focus ~15 km deep near Barpak, rupture ~140 km eastwards on the Main Himalayan Thrust; PGA in Kathmandu only ~0.16g but strong 4–5 s basin resonance; about 8,970 deaths.
Gravitational waves are ripples of spacetime travelling at c, of strain h = Δ L/L ≈ 10^-21. LIGO's 4 km interferometers detected GW150914 on 14 September 2015 (36 + 29 → 62 solar masses, 3 radiated).
Nanotechnology works between 1 and 100 nm, where surface-to-volume ratio (6/L) and quantum confinement change behaviour: fullerenes, nanotubes, graphene, quantum dots.
The Higgs field gives elementary particles their mass; its quantum, the Higgs boson (≈ 125 GeV/c^2, spin 0), was found at the LHC on 4 July 2012.
